title: Station ALOHA lost 10% of its 300-700 m oxygen stock proxy, with 69% of the loss at fixed density
abstract: Does oxygen loss on one density surface imply a stock loss across a depth range? We use finalized Hawaii Ocean Time-series bottle data to test this at Station ALOHA. The 300-700 m oxygen stock proxy fell from 47.75 to 42.93 mol/m2 between 1989-1996 and 2009-2024, a loss of 10.1%. The change is -4.82 mol/m2 (95% year-bootstrap interval -6.54 to -3.09). A fixed early oxygen-density curve evaluated at observed density profiles gives a density-displacement change of -1.50 mol/m2. The residual is -3.32 mol/m2, or 69% (53-91%) of the loss. The upper 100 umol/kg crossing became 39 m shallower. The loss persists across bottle-gap, depth-range, seasonal and block-bootstrap checks. Same-cruise deep references retain most of the separate oxygen decline on density 26.5. This extends a concentration result to a local column stock diagnostic. The proxy assumes water density of 1026 kg/m3. The residual can include water mix, ventilation and respiration. One station does not give a basin inventory or prove an outcrop cause.

display.caption: ALOHA oxygen stock proxy at 300-700 m, profile changes, and their additive density-displacement decomposition. Early years are 1989-1996; late years are 2009-2024. Error bars are 95% year-bootstrap intervals.

citations.reason: We reuse its HOT parser and exact source file hashes, and extend its single-surface result to a local stock diagnostic.
Its BATS concentration and inventory result motivates the local stock test.
The local stock loss is consistent with its North Pacific ventilation mechanism, but does not establish cause.
Its tracer-calibrated ventilation model is context. We do not run or fit it here.
